design:
# Deep Extraction + Streaming Design: MQL5 Part 69 Flag Pattern Detection (lynnchris)

**Task**: New research (sibling to quantwave-bfg)  
**Completed**: 2026-05-30 IST  
**Article**: Part 69 of the Price Action Analysis Toolkit series

## Primary Sources (recorded)
- Article: https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/22503  
  "Price Action Analysis Toolkit Development (Part 69): Flag Pattern Detection in MQL5" by Christian Benjamin (lynnchris), published ~19-21 May 2026.
- Download ZIP: https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/download/22503.zip (confirmed working 2026-05-30)
- Local persisted source: `references/MQL5/lynnchris/Part69/Flag_Pattern_Detector.mq5` (29,628 bytes, 823 lines, archive date 2026-05-19)
- Follow-on: Part 70 (https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/22607) turns the detector signals into EA execution (buffer-based iCustom consumption).
- Series hub: https://www.mql5.com/en/users/lynnchris/publications
- Linked in project: Discovered from user request after bfg (Part 66) + cu03 geometric scope (ej8b explicitly covers "Flags + H&S").

**Key quote from code header**:
```
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//|                                        Flag_Pattern_Detector.mq5 |
//|                              Copyright 2026, Christian Benjamin. |
//|                          https://www.mql5.com/en/users/lynnchris |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Article intent (from summaries + code)**:
"converts subjective visual flag (continuation) pattern recognition into objective, reproducible MQL5 logic." Strict structural filtering (pole impulse, retracement %, pullback/push count, breakout in pole direction) rather than loose matching. Tested on EURUSD M5 and synthetic indices.

## Input Parameters (exact + comments)
```mql5
input int      LookbackBars      =2000;        // Bars to scan backward (first load only)
input double   MinPoleATR        =1.0;         // Minimum flagpole size (ATR multiple)
input double   MaxRetracePercent =61.8;        // Max retracement of flag (% of pole)
input int      MinFlagBars       =4;           // Minimum flag duration
input int      MaxFlagBars       =0;           // Max flag duration (0 = no limit)
input bool     DebugMode         =true;        // Print detected flags to Experts tab
input color    BullFlagColor     =clrDodgerBlue;
input color    BearFlagColor     =clrTomato;

// alert parameters (EnableAlerts, EnableSound, SoundFile, EnableNotification, EnableEmail)
```
ATR handle: hard-coded period **20** in OnInit (different from H&S 14).

## Core Structures
```mql5
struct DrawnFlag   // historical completed (for dedup + overlap prevention)
  {
   int poleStart, poleEnd, flagStart, flagEnd;
   datetime startTime, endTime;
   bool isBull;
  };

struct ActiveFlag  // live in-flight patterns with counters
  {
   int poleStart, poleEnd, flagStart, lastUpdate;
   bool isBull;
   double poleHigh, poleLow, poleLength, extreme;
   int pullbacks, pushes;
   datetime poleStartTime, poleEndTime;
  };
```

Two arrays: `drawnFlags[]` and `activeFlags[]`.

## Algorithm Pipeline (high-fidelity)

**Cold start (prev_calculated == 0)**:
- `ScanHistoricalFlags(...)`: from rates_total - LookbackBars, repeatedly call `FindThreeBarMove`, then for each pole compute flagStart...lastBar, validate retrace + pullbacks>pushes + duration, then continue scanning forward until breakout or invalidation? (the scan path builds completed flags when breakout is detected during the historical pass).

**Incremental (prev_calculated > 0)**:
- For each new bar: 
  - Update all existing ActiveFlags (check breakout on pole extreme breach, update extreme + retrace + push/pull counts).
  - On breakout: IsTooClose check → DrawSlantedPattern + RecordDrawnFlag + alert → remove from active.
  - Scan only recent 5 bars for new 3-bar poles → TryAddActiveFlag.

**Pole detection — `FindThreeBarMove`** (the distinctive "flagpole" primitive):
- Scans forward from startIndex looking for a 3-bar sequence where total directional body (close-open sum for up or open-close for down) > atr[j] * MinPoleATR.
- Returns the 3-bar window as the pole (moveStart to moveEnd = +2).

**Flag creation / validation — `TryAddActiveFlag`**:
- Reject if pole already drawn or active.
- Compute poleHigh/poleLow/poleLength from the 3-bar extremes (direction-aware).
- flagStart = poleEnd + 1
- Immediate initial retrace check against current extreme (must be <= MaxRetracePercent of pole).
- Count pullbacks vs pushes so far (pullback = counter-trend bar extreme).
- Require pullbacks > pushes (classic flag "consolidation under pressure").
- Duration >= MinFlagBars (and <= Max if set).
- If all pass: create ActiveFlag with current counters and extreme, add to activeFlags[].

**Live update — `UpdateActiveFlag`**:
- Skip if bar <= lastUpdate.
- Check breakout: bull flag close > poleHigh, bear close < poleLow.
- On breakout: IsTooClose (30% overlap or bar proximity) → if ok, draw + record + alert + return true (caller removes it).
- No breakout: update extreme (new low for bull flag, new high for bear), recompute retrace %, continue counting pullbacks/pushes on the new bar.
- (There is also a `ValidateFlagConsolidation` helper used in the historical full scan path with the same rules.)

**Overlap / dedup — `IsTooClose`**:
- Exact (flagStart, flagEnd) match, or >30% bar overlap, or very close start/end bars (±2-3).

**Drawing — `DrawSlantedPattern`** (sophisticated geometry):
- Pole: solid OBJ_TREND (2px, color by direction).
- Slanted parallel channel: estimates slope from highest-highs (bull) or lowest-lows (bear) in first vs second half of consolidation, forces slight counter-slope if needed, draws two parallel OBJ_TREND lines + a filled OBJ_RECTANGLE zone.
- Breakout arrow + text label ("Bullish Flag" / "Bearish Flag").
- Unique prefix "Flag_<poleStart>_<poleEnd>_" + ObjectsDeleteAll on that prefix before redraw.
- Much more geometric effort than the H&S triangle regions.

**ATR**: 20-period (different from H&S Part 66's 14).

## Comparison vs Part 66 H&S (lynnchris series — very useful for cu03 geometric work)

**Similarities (same author philosophy)**:
- Both are purely graphical (no buffers/plots).
- Heavy use of chart objects with prefix-based cleanup.
- Same alert + DebugMode patterns.
- Strong emphasis on deduplication / overlap prevention.
- Both maintain "completed/drawn" history + active/in-flight state.
- Both ultimately emit on **breakout** of the pattern structure.
- Same "chart objects are the output" trap (Part 70 lesson applies equally).

**Important differences** (Flags is more streaming-friendly):
- **Pole primitive**: H&S uses general local swings (SwingStrength=3 window). Flags uses a very specific **3-bar directional body impulse > ATR*MinPoleATR**. Much narrower and "impulse-first".
- **State machine**: Flags has a proper `ActiveFlag` with live counters (pullbacks/pushes/extreme) that is updated bar-by-bar. H&S was more "find 5-swing sequence then score once".
- **Retracement model**: Flags = % of pole (Fib 61.8 classic). H&S = absolute shoulder symmetry tolerance.
- **Validation inside pattern**: Flags explicitly counts "more pullbacks than pushes" (continuation pressure). H&S uses time + price symmetry + slope + size scoring.
- **Incremental design**: Flags already respects `prev_calculated` and only does small recent-bar scans for new poles + updates active list. H&S did full re-detection of swings every bar.
- **Geometry**: Flags builds slanted parallel channels + rectangle zone (more sophisticated "channel" view of consolidation). H&S used filled triangles on the three swings + simple neckline.
- **ATR periods**: 20 (flags) vs 14 (H&S).
- **Historical scan**: Flags has explicit LookbackBars cold-start path + separate active scan. H&S was simpler full-history every time.

**Implication for QuantWave**:
The Flags implementation is **closer to a proper streaming state machine** already. The pole → active consolidation tracker → breakout watcher pattern maps very cleanly to `Next<T>` (ActiveFlag becomes the internal state of a streaming FlagDetector struct).

## Streaming Design Sketch for QuantWave (recommended approach)

**Preferred architecture** (consistent with bfg recommendation):
1. Shared Swing / Impulse detector (or reuse/extend the MarketStructure swing work from cu03-iuzv + a specialized 3-bar impulse detector for flagpoles).
2. FlagDetector as a consumer:
   - Maintains a small ring buffer of recent "pole events" (3-bar impulses that met MinPoleATR).
   - On new bar or new swing: for each recent unconsolidated pole, maintain an ActiveFlag-like struct (extreme, pullback/push counters, current retrace %).
   - On each bar: update all active flags (retrace, counters). Emit rich event on valid breakout (after IsTooClose / overlap check).
   - Optional: a separate historical batch path for cold-start Lookback using the same validation rules.

**Rich output struct** (for backtester / ML):
```rust
pub struct FlagPattern {
    pub id: u32,
    pub is_bull: bool,
    pub pole_start: BarRef,
    pub pole_end: BarRef,
    pub flag_start: BarRef,
    pub flag_end: BarRef,           // breakout bar on completion
    pub pole_length: f64,
    pub pole_length_atr: f64,       // MinPoleATR context
    pub max_retrace_pct: f64,       // actual max retrace observed
    pub pullbacks: i32,
    pub pushes: i32,
    pub breakout_confirmed: bool,
    pub breakout_price: f64,
    // metadata useful for sizing / conviction
    pub consolidation_bars: i32,
    pub pole_strength: f64,         // actual body sum / ATR at pole
}
```

**Invariants** (examples):
- pole body sum (directional) > MinPoleATR * ATR at pole time.
- max retrace during flag <= MaxRetracePercent of pole.
- pullbacks > pushes throughout the flag (until breakout).
- breakout occurs by breaching the pole extreme in the original direction.
- No two drawn flags have >30% overlap or near-identical (start,end) per IsTooClose rules.
- Streaming vs batch produce identical poleStart/poleEnd + flagStart/flagEnd (within boundary tolerance).

**Synthetic ideas**:
- Generate clean 3-bar impulse pole (strong body sum), then controlled retracement with more counter-trend extremes than with-trend (pullbacks > pushes), duration 5-15 bars, then clean breakout.
- Inject violations (retrace > 61.8%, more pushes than pullbacks, short duration, weak pole) → must be rejected.
- Overlapping candidate flags → dedup keeps the first valid or the one with cleanest metrics.
- Combine with existing regime synthetics (flags are continuation patterns — expect higher quality in strong regime states).

## Cross-References to QuantWave + cu03
- Directly feeds `quantwave-ej8b` (Geometric Pattern Detectors child under cu03) alongside the H&S work from bfg.
- Pole detection (3-bar impulse) is a new primitive not present in current fractals/rodc — can be a small reusable component or folded into the shared SwingAnalyzer.
- The ActiveFlag state machine (counters + extreme tracking + breakout watcher) is an excellent model for any "consolidation/continuation" detector.
- Same rich-struct + backtester metadata needs as H&S (pole strength for conviction, retrace depth, pullback count as features).
- Visualization is again secondary — we must emit the struct first.

## Risks / Improvements We Will Make
- Same object-drawing-as-primary-output problem (Part 70 lesson).
- ATR period hard-coded (20 here).
- LookbackBars full scan on cold start — we will make the batch path clean and parity-guaranteed.
- "3-bar body sum" pole is quite specific; we may expose it or generalize to "N-bar impulse > k*ATR".
- Overlap logic (IsTooClose) is heuristic (30% + proximity) — we will make the rules explicit and tunable or document the exact port.

## Recommended Tracking & Next Steps
- This report should be attached to (or used to create) a dedicated research task sibling to quantwave-bfg, discovered-from b7u / cu03.
- Once both bfg (H&S) and this Flags extraction are in bd, the geometric implementation child (ej8b) has solid, source-recorded foundations for both patterns.
- Prioritize the shared swing/impulse foundation (iuzv) — both H&S and Flags become much cleaner on top of it.
- Consider a small "ImpulseDetector" or "PoleDetector" primitive that both (and future patterns) can reuse.

This completes the "run the same way" request for Part 69. All logic, parameters, state machines, and drawing details extracted from the authoritative .mq5 source. Ready for implementation planning under the cu03 geometric epic.

title: Enforce the parity-proptest + gold-fixture pattern per indicator (meta-check in CI)
description:
PROBLEM
~140 indicator files in quantwave-core/src/indicators/ carry a streaming-vs-batch parity
proptest by convention, and 27 gold fixtures exist — but nothing enforces that a NEW indicator
ships with either. The griffiths_spectrum incident (gold test commented out when its fixture was
lost) proves coverage can silently vanish. Batch↔streaming parity is the product's core promise;
it must be structurally guaranteed, not cultural.
design:
1. Add an xtask check (quantwave-xtask is nearly empty — 48 LOC — good home): walk the compiled
   indicator registry (every type with IndicatorMetadata) and assert for each: (a) a proptest
   parity block exists in its source file (parse for `proptest!` in the module, or better: a
   registry of parity tests emitted by a macro), (b) a gold fixture exists under

   (tests/parity_exemptions.toml) with a written justification.
2. Wire into ci.yml sanity job (cheap — no test execution, just presence checking).
3. First run produces the TRUE current coverage list; existing gaps (e.g. griffiths until its
   fixture is regenerated) seed the exemptions file with justifications and follow-up issue IDs.
4. Publish the resulting coverage stats as a generated artifact (feeds G2's validation page).
acceptance_criteria:
TDD
1. Run the check on current main → it must produce the real gap list (expect griffiths + a
   handful); those entries go into the exemptions file with justifications — that file is a
   deliverable of this issue.
2. Negative test: add a dummy indicator with IndicatorMetadata and NO proptest on a scratch
   branch → CI check MUST fail.
3. Exemption without a justification string → check MUST fail (schema validation).

title: Lock in zero-unsafe / zero-panic core with workspace lint enforcement
description:
PROBLEM
quantwave-core currently has 0 unsafe blocks, 0 panic! calls, and unwraps confined to test

session) from introducing them. Additionally 89 #[allow(...)] attributes are scattered across
crates, dominated by non_camel_case_types in talib_wrapper.rs (legitimate FFI naming, but
spread ad hoc).
design:
1. Add a [workspace.lints] table in root Cargo.toml, inherited by member crates:
   - forbid(unsafe_code) in quantwave-core, quantwave-polars, quantwave-backtest (allow only in
     FFI crates where genuinely required, each with a comment).
   - deny clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used, clippy::panic for core + backtest
     production code (cfg(test) allows via clippy.toml allow-unwrap-in-tests = true).
2. Consolidate talib_wrapper.rs bulk allows to a single module-level allow with an explanatory
   comment.
3. DEPENDENCY: quantwave-backtest must be de-panicked first (BAD epic B4) or its lints start as
   warn with a tracked flip-to-deny; core can go straight to deny.
4. Effective only with the CI clippy gate (BAD epic B1) running -D warnings.
acceptance_criteria:
TDD
1. Negative test: introduce an unsafe block in quantwave-core on a scratch branch → CI clippy
   MUST fail. Same for a production-path unwrap.
2. cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings green on main after the change.
ACCEPTANCE
- Lints live in root Cargo.toml; violations impossible to merge once B1's gate is active.

title: Release invariants in CI — verify artifacts before they ship (protect the release engineering)
description:
PROBLEM
The release pipeline is genuinely well-structured (ordered crates.io publish core→backtest/
plugins→polars→quantwave via scripts/publish_crates.sh; real 4-platform wheel matrix) — but it
has ZERO self-verification of what it builds. The UGLY-epic wheel-tag bug shipped precisely
because nothing inspects built artifacts before PyPI upload. Good machinery, no guardrails.
design:
1. Gate release.yml uploads on scripts/verify_wheel_tags.py (built in the UGLY wheel-fix issue):
   tag/content compatibility for every wheel in the matrix.
2. Add twine check + a clean-container import smoke test per platform artifact
   (pip install <wheel>; python -c "import quantwave, quantwave_plugins; ..."), before upload.
3. Add cargo publish --dry-run for each crate in publish order, run on PRs that touch any crate
   version (catches broken manifests/missing files before release day).
4. Optional: a Test-PyPI dry-run stage for release candidates.
5. Document the invariants in .github/workflows/README.md.
acceptance_criteria:
TDD
1. Negative fixture: keep one deliberately-bad merged wheel (py3-none tag + cpXY .so) as a test
   fixture; the verifier's own test suite must reject it (tests the tester).
2. Dry-run publish job green on a version-bump PR; red when a crate manifest is broken
   (verify once with an intentional break on a branch).
ACCEPTANCE
- No artifact reaches PyPI/crates.io without passing tag verification + import smoke;
  workflows README documents the invariant chain.

title: Ratio metrics return inf or noise on thin trade counts with no signal to the caller
description:
Verified against 0.7.0. A single-trade backtest returned sharpe_ratio 7.98, sortino_ratio inf, profit_factor inf, win_rate 1.0 -- every headline metric reading as a spectacular strategy off one winning trade worth 2 dollars. .metrics() gives no indication that the sample is too thin for these ratios to mean anything, and num_trades sits alongside them as just another key rather than as a precondition.

This interacts badly with the 1-unit sizing default (quantwave-9wji): the same run reports total_return 2e-05, so a user sees a near-zero return next to a 7.98 Sharpe and has no way to tell which number to believe. Neither is meaningful.

Deliverables: (a) return NaN rather than inf for sortino_ratio and profit_factor when the denominator is empty (no losing trades / no downside), since inf reads as a value and NaN reads as undefined; (b) consider a .metrics() warning or a diagnostics accessor when num_trades is below a documented threshold (~30); (c) document in the output contract that ratio metrics are unreliable below that count. Note the 10-key .metrics() contract is test-enforced and must not gain or lose keys -- any warning surface has to be additive, e.g. on .extended_metrics() or a separate accessor.
close_reason: sortino_ratio and profit_factor now return NaN instead of inf when the denominator is empty (no losing trades / no downside deviation); empty-series 0.0 convention preserved. Added MIN_TRADES_FOR_RELIABLE_RATIOS=30 named constant and a MetricsDiagnostics surface exposing low_sample_size, num_trades, threshold, undefined_metrics and human-readable warnings — reachable via .diagnostics() on BacktestResult/BacktestReport and extended_metrics()['diagnostics']. 10-key .metrics() contract untouched: verified 10 keys exactly, no 'diagnostics' leak, and the enforcing test file is purely additive (zero deleted lines). Deduplicated two identical inf-producing branches in from_raw and aggregate_trade_stats into compute_profit_factor. Docs: output-contract.md, capability_matrix.md. Verified independently after rebuilding the extension: 846 Rust tests pass, 392 Python pass, fmt+clippy clean. Five tests changed comparison operator only (NaN != NaN broke whole-bundle equality) — assert_same_metrics still compares full key sets and every value, no expected numeric value altered. Side benefit: walk_forward selection no longer lets an inf-scoring degenerate no-losing-trades variant win, since NaN never compares greater. calmar_ratio still returns inf and was out of scope — split to quantwave-gz7d. Branch fix/quantwave-s3iu-nan-ratios-and-thin-sample-diagnostics, not merged.

title: Benchmarks Nightly fails on main: harness.py to_pandas() needs pyarrow, not installed in the workflow
description:
Scheduled run 30739618434 on main failed 2026-08-02 08:28 UTC. Failing every night, so the published benchmark numbers are not being refreshed.

  File "benchmarks/harness.py", line 42, in memory_benchmark
    pdf = df.select(["open","high","low","close","volume","symbol"]).to_pandas()
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named pyarrow

polars .to_pandas() delegates to pyarrow, which is an optional polars dependency and is not installed in the Benchmarks Nightly workflow. The build succeeded; only the harness step failed, so this is purely a missing test-time dependency.

Fix options: (a) add pyarrow to whatever the workflow installs (a requirements file or an explicit pip install step) -- simplest and keeps the pandas-comparison benchmark meaningful; (b) if the memory benchmark only needs a pandas frame for the footprint comparison, use polars .to_pandas(use_pyarrow_extension_array=False) and confirm whether that still routes through pyarrow on this polars version, or build the pandas frame without polars conversion. Note this benchmark is what backs the README claim of 2-5x lower memory footprint vs pandas, so it should keep comparing against a genuine pandas frame rather than being stubbed out.

Also worth adding: fail the workflow loudly on import errors at startup rather than mid-harness, so a missing dep is obvious.
notes:
ROOT CAUSE CORRECTED 2026-08-12. The nightly has failed every run since 2026-07-12, but for TWO different causes, and the second was hidden behind the first.

(1) 2026-07-12 .. 2026-08-02 -- failed at step 'Run benchmark harness (1M rows)': the missing pyarrow this issue was filed for. FIXED and confirmed.

(2) 2026-08-09 onward (runs 31297120506, 31299876202) -- fails at step 'Commit results if changed'. Not the harness at all. The push to main is rejected by the 'main protect' ruleset (id 18785336):
    remote: error: GH013: Repository rule violations found for refs/heads/main
    remote: - Changes must be made through a pull request.
    remote: - Required status check 'Doc & metadata sanity' is expected.
bypass_actors on that ruleset was null, so github-actions[bot] had no exemption and the workflow could never succeed as written. Compounding it, the commit message carries [skip ci], so the required check would never report even if the PR rule were satisfied -- a deadlock by construction.

MY EARLIER DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: I attributed the failure to a push race and added a rebase-retry loop. That loop retries a categorically forbidden push three times. It is kept (a real race IS possible -- the harness runs for minutes and main can move) but its comment now states plainly that it does NOT address GH013, so the next person does not misread it the way I did.

FIX (owner decision 2026-08-12, option a): add the GitHub Actions app (integration id 15368) as an 'Always' bypass actor on ruleset 18785336. Repo configuration, done by the owner -- not something the workflow can arrange.

RELATED: quantwave-5yjg (non-deterministic frame_hash) means every run produces a diff regardless of whether the numbers moved, so once pushes work this will commit weekly no-ops until 5yjg is fixed.

title: ta_* plugins take (high, low, close) — reorder to match their siblings; they are native Rust, not wrappers
description:
P0 because it returns a wrong number with no error, on the surface users reach for specifically when they want TA-Lib-identical values.

THE TRAP. .ta.atr puts close in the receiver. The ta_-prefixed twin needs high in the receiver, because the TA-Lib signature it mirrors is ATR(high, low, close). Writing it the way its sibling reads — the obvious way — permutes the inputs. Re-verified on main after the 0.7.0 merges, against a hand-computed Wilder RMA of 1.384819 on a 200-bar random walk:

  pl.col("high").ta.ta_atr("low","close",14)  = 1.384819   correct
  pl.col("close").ta.ta_atr("high","low",14)  = 1.252823   WRONG, no error, 9.5% off
  pl.col("close").ta.atr("high","low",14)     = 1.384819   sibling, close in receiver

All three arguments are equal-length f64 columns, so permuting them is type-valid and nothing can raise. Error magnitude is data-dependent, so it never looks obviously broken. ATR feeds stop distance and vol-target sizing, so it propagates straight into risk.

CORRECTED FRAMING (this issue previously implied an FFI constraint — it does not exist). The ta_* surface is NOT a TA-Lib wrapper. TaATR is native Rust: quantwave-core/src/indicators/incremental/ta_atr.rs, "Native O(1) ATR — TA-Lib Wilder smoothing on true range", implementing Next<T>, with talib_rs appearing only in a doc comment. The ta_ prefix denotes the TA-Lib CONVENTION (Wilder RMA), not a binding. Argument order was inherited from the generated signature, not forced by an external API.

THEREFORE THE FIX IS TO REMOVE THE TRAP, NOT DOCUMENT IT. Reorder the multi-input ta_* plugins so the receiver matches their non-prefixed sibling (close in receiver, high/low as args). Nothing external constrains this. Breaking for anyone currently calling them correctly, so it needs a changelog entry and a release note — but the population calling them correctly today is small, and the population silently getting wrong numbers is the one worth protecting.

Deliverables:
(a) Reorder multi-input ta_* plugins to match sibling receiver semantics. Audit the whole ta_* set, not just ta_atr — the signatures are code-generated from one template so ta_natr, ta_trange and the rest share the shape.
(b) Rename the generated params from in2/in3 to real semantic names (high/low/close) so the call site is self-documenting and keyword arguments become possible. This is what made the bug invisible: there is nothing in the signature to key off.
(c) Add tests pinning each multi-input ta_* against a hand-computed or oracle reference IN THE DOCUMENTED CALL ORDER.
(d) Fix the generator, not just the output — see quantwave-0h4o, where the same generator emits a blanket timeperiod=14 default that contradicts TA-Lib per-function defaults (BETA 5, CORREL 30).

Docs to update once landed: guides/plugin_vs_ta.md and guides/talib_migration.md both describe ta_* in wrapper terms; the shipped agent skill .claude/skills/quantwave/PITFALLS.md section 5 documents the trap and must switch to documenting the corrected order.
close_reason:
Fixed and shipped on main. ta_atr, ta_natr and ta_trange now take close in the receiver, matching their non-prefixed siblings; parameters renamed from the generated in2/in3 to high/low so a mis-ordered call is visible at the call site and keyword args work.

Verified: pl.col(close).ta.ta_atr(high,low,14) now returns 1.384819, equal to a hand-computed Wilder RMA and to its sibling pl.col(close).ta.atr(high,low,14). Before the fix that natural call returned 1.252823 -- about 10 percent off, data-dependent, and unable to raise because all three arguments are equal-length f64 columns.

SCOPE WAS NARROWER THAN THIS ISSUE ASSUMED. It said the problem was almost certainly wider than ta_atr because the signatures are generated. In fact only the three 3-input plugins invert: ta_atr, ta_natr, ta_trange. ta_beta and ta_correl take (self, other) -- already the same shape as their siblings -- and needed only the in2 to other rename. The five single-input ta_* were never affected.

Deliverables:
(a) receiver reordered on the three 3-input plugins - done
(b) semantic parameter names replacing in2/in3 - done
(c) tests pinning the documented call order - tests/python/test_ta_prefixed_arg_order.py, 8 tests, every assertion anchored to values computed independently in the test file rather than to current behaviour, including a guard asserting the OLD receiver order is now the wrong one so a silent revert fails
(d) generator fixed, not just its output - scripts/gen_pyo3_plugins_py.py templates corrected, so regenerating cannot reintroduce this

Also updated test_conventions.py, which had encoded the old order (intent preserved), and the shipped agent skill: PITFALLS.md section 5 now leads with the surviving trap - the same slug meaning different math on different surfaces - with the argument order demoted to a historical note, and its linter rule inverted to flag the old order.

BREAKING for anyone who was calling these correctly with high in the receiver; changelog entry added under Unreleased with a before/after snippet.

Verified: 1107 Rust tests, 451 pytest, 15/15 doc gate. Related quantwave-0h4o (ta_* twins disagree on default periods) is the same generator's doing and remains open.

title: Decide whether indicators should emit null instead of NaN for warmup
description:
Option (a) split out of quantwave-4rsq, which shipped the non-breaking mitigations (trim_warmup helper + .bt warning). This is the open architectural decision.

FINDING: this is a multi-week architecture change, not a mechanical sweep, and the 221-indicator parity sweep is the CHEAP part.

Root tension: batch and streaming share one code path by design. Next<Input> is fn next(&mut self, input: Input) -> Self::Output with Output = f64 for scalar indicators. Nulls do not exist in that trait -- only the Polars column layer can express them. Bit-identical batch/streaming parity is a headline guarantee. So there are two shapes:

(1) Null only at the Polars layer -- keep f64::NAN in core, mask to null when building the Series. Cheapest, but FORKS the semantics the library sells: lf.ta.rsi(14) returns null while streaming_class("rsi").next(x) returns NaN, and assert_parity must learn a null<->NaN equivalence. Costs a validity-mask pass per output column.

(2) Output = Option<f64> through the core -- semantically correct and uniform, but breaks the public Rust trait implemented across ~124 core files, cascading into PyO3 (24 files), the WASM crate, and every downstream Vec<f64> consumer.

Surface count of NaN-bearing lines: quantwave-core 847 lines / 124 files; quantwave-py 463 / 24; quantwave-polars 153 / 2; quantwave-backtest 10 / 2.

Long tail, where the real risk sits:
- Multi-output indicators (MACD, BBANDS, Ichimoku, SuperTrend) have PER-FIELD warmups, so null-ness becomes per-field, not per-row.
- Mid-series NaN is NOT warmup. Some indicators emit NaN on degenerate input (zero variance, division by zero) long after warmup. If those become null too, drop_nulls() starts silently punching holes in the MIDDLE of a frame -- arguably a worse footgun than the one being fixed.
- The 11 zero-warmup indicators (kalman_filter, mama, sar, frac_diff, market_structure, ...) have no metadata warmup, so leading-null-ness is not derivable from metadata; each needs individual inspection.
- Downstream breakage is broad: backtest engine, build_feature_matrix, the talib array API, and every notebook example assume float columns with no validity mask. Null-propagating arithmetic differs from NaN-propagating (null > 30 is null, not false -- which changes signal columns, arguably for the better, but changes them).

RECOMMENDATION: if this proceeds, take shape (1) behind an opt-in first -- a null_warmup=True kwarg or a global qw.set_warmup_policy("null") -- shipped for one minor version so the parity harness and docs migrate before it becomes default. A big-bang default flip across 221 indicators is where the risk concentrates.

title: Fill metadata: Ehlers Filters batch (super_smoother, roofing_filter, gaussian, hamming, hann, triangle, butterworth, high_pass, instantaneous_trendline, laguerre_filter, classic_laguerre)
description:
Epic: quantwave-e0c. Fill usage/keywords/ehlers_summary stubs in each file under quantwave-core/src/indicators/. Field order in struct: description → usage → keywords → ehlers_summary → params. Use sed or direct file edit.

super_smoother.rs: usage='Use as a drop-in replacement for any MA when maximum smoothing with minimal lag is needed. Ideal pre-filter before oscillators to eliminate high-frequency noise.' keywords=&["filter","smoothing","ehlers","dsp","low-pass"] ehlers_summary='Ehlers describes the SuperSmoother as a 2-pole Butterworth filter achieving the same smoothing as a longer SMA with far less lag. It uses a critically-damped design to eliminate Gibbs phenomenon overshoot while retaining cycle information.'

roofing_filter.rs: usage='Apply before oscillators to remove both low-frequency trend drift and high-frequency noise, leaving only the tradable cycle band (10-48 bars).' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","cycle","high-pass","low-pass"] ehlers_summary='Introduced in Cycle Analytics for Traders (2013), the Roofing Filter first applies a high-pass filter to remove trend, then a SuperSmoother to remove noise. The result is a cycle-only signal with controlled bandwidth ideal for oscillator inputs.'

gaussian.rs: usage='Use when smooth symmetric price averaging with near-zero phase shift is needed. Works well as preprocessing for spectral analysis.' keywords=&["filter","smoothing","ehlers","dsp","low-pass"] ehlers_summary='Gaussian filters minimize the time-bandwidth product. Ehlers implements them as cascaded pole filters with Gaussian-derived coefficients, achieving smooth output with excellent stopband attenuation and no ripple.'

hamming.rs: usage='Apply as a windowing function before DFT-based cycle detection to reduce sidelobe leakage and obtain cleaner dominant cycle estimates.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","windowing","spectral"] ehlers_summary='The Hamming window is a raised-cosine weighting function that reduces spectral leakage. Ehlers uses it in DFT cycle measurement to prevent energy in one frequency bin from contaminating adjacent bins.'

hann.rs: usage='Use as windowing before FFT-based dominant cycle measurement to achieve clean spectral separation between market cycles.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","windowing","spectral"] ehlers_summary='The Hann window provides a smooth bell-shaped taper achieving -31.5 dB first sidelobe suppression. In Cycle Analytics for Traders Ehlers uses it as the preferred DFT window for the best trade-off between frequency resolution and leakage rejection.'

triangle.rs: usage='Use as a pre-smoother to reduce noise before applying cycle or momentum indicators when symmetric low-ripple response is needed.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","smoothing","triangle"] ehlers_summary='The Triangle (Bartlett) window is a linearly-tapered FIR filter equivalent to applying two rectangular windows in sequence. It provides moderate sidelobe suppression and is useful when computational simplicity is preferred over maximum attenuation.'

butterworth.rs: usage='Use to smooth price or indicator values with a flat passband and sharp rolloff. The 3-pole version provides steeper attenuation at the cost of marginally more lag.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","smoothing","low-pass"] ehlers_summary='Butterworth filters are maximally flat in the passband introducing no ripple. Ehlers implements 2-pole and 3-pole Butterworth IIR designs in Cycle Analytics for Traders, noting the SuperSmoother is a critically-damped 2-pole Butterworth variant.'

high_pass.rs: usage='Apply to price to isolate the cyclical component by attenuating the low-frequency trend. Use as the first stage before an oscillator or spectrum analyser.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","high-pass","cycle"] ehlers_summary='Ehlers derives the 1-pole high-pass filter in Cycle Analytics for Traders analogously to EMA derivation but applied to differences. It removes the DC component and trend, leaving cyclical content for downstream analysis.'

instantaneous_trendline.rs: usage='Use as an adaptive trend line that automatically adjusts to the current dominant cycle period, replacing fixed-period moving averages in trend-following systems.' keywords=&["trend","adaptive","moving-average","ehlers","dsp"] ehlers_summary='Defined in Rocket Science for Traders (2001), the Instantaneous Trendline is derived from Hilbert Transform phasors and synchronized to the current market cycle. It is computed as a 3-bar weighted average adjusted by the instantaneous period, giving a zero-lag trend estimate.'

laguerre_filter.rs: usage='Use as a low-lag smoothing filter with only 4 elements of state. Ideal when memory-efficiency matters or when a highly responsive smoother for real-time streaming is needed.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","smoothing","laguerre"] ehlers_summary='Ehlers introduces Laguerre filters in Cybernetic Analysis (2004), noting they achieve the response of much longer conventional filters using only four coefficients. The gamma parameter controls the lag-smoothness trade-off.'

classic_laguerre.rs: usage='Use when a smooth trend estimate with controllable lag using only 4 state variables is needed. Preferred over long EMAs when computational memory is constrained.' keywords=&["filter","ehlers","dsp","smoothing","laguerre"] ehlers_summary='The Classic Laguerre Filter uses four first-order IIR sections sharing the same gamma coefficient. In Cybernetic Analysis (2004) Ehlers shows gamma maps directly to an effective period, making it highly tunable with minimal computation.'

title: Epic: Rewrite talib wrappers as native O(1) state machines
description:
Currently, indicators wrapped from `talib-rs` (like RSI, MACD, etc.) suffer from O(N²) streaming performance because the wrapper must buffer all history and re-execute the batch C-level function on every tick. We need to rewrite these indicators natively in `quantwave-core` to use our optimized `RingBuffer` and O(1) mathematical updates.

Scope:
- Rewrite high-priority indicators first (RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, ATR, etc.) to be native state machines (like our native SMA).
- Eventually cover all 151 wrapped indicators.
- Replace the legacy `talib_1_in_1_out!` macro wrappers with native structs implementing the `Next` trait.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Performance Benchmarking: Streaming 100k rows must drop from ~14-18 seconds down to sub-millisecond ranges (comparable to our native SMA which takes ~230 µs).
- Mandatory Parity Testing: The existing property-based tests MUST pass. The native implementation MUST match `talib-rs` batch outputs perfectly (using `approx` bit-level equivalence).
- Clean up unused wrappers once native versions are verified and stable.
- Ensure the newly native indicators are seamlessly exposed to the `quantwave-polars` extension.

title: hmm_bull_bear: silent constant-Bull on price-scale input (emission params assume returns); undocumented {1,2} labels
description: Dogfood finding 5. hmm_bull_bear returns a constant 1 when fed PRICE (uptrend/downtrend/real index all read as bull); it only varies on RETURNS input, and then emits states {1,2} not {0,1}, with 2 empirically bear. More seriously it appears to batch-fit over the whole series, which is look-ahead and makes it unusable in a backtest -- needs a causal/streaming fit. Deliverables: causal fit path, plus docs clarifying the input contract (returns not price) and the state-label meaning. Locate the implementation (not found under the hmm_bull_bear slug in a quick grep; likely in the regimes module under a different symbol name).
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST CODE 2026-08-11 (main d29b96dd4): the look-ahead premise is WRONG. quantwave-py/src/plugins/custom_4.rs:47 hmm_bull_bear loops i in 0..len feeding one value at a time into core::regimes::hmm::HMM (online Viterbi, hardcoded params, no Baum-Welch, no batch fit). It is strictly causal. hmm.rs is 138 lines with no fit path at all.

Real root cause of the 'constant 1 on price' symptom is emission-parameter scale, not look-ahead. HMM::bull_bear() hardcodes means [0.001, -0.002] and stds [0.01, 0.02] -- daily RETURNS. Feed a price like 100.0 and gaussian_pdf underflows to 0.0 for BOTH states, so next_delta = ln(0) = -inf for both. The comparison next_delta[j] > max_prob is false when both are -inf, so best_state stays 0 => Bull => constant 1 forever.

Labels: custom_4.rs:56-60 maps Bull=>1, Bear=>2, Cluster/other=>0. So {1,2} is deliberate, with 0 reserved. Not a bug, but undocumented.

RESCOPE: this is not a multi-week causal-fit rewrite. Deliverables are (1) reject or warn on non-return-scale input instead of silently emitting constant Bull, (2) document the returns-not-price contract, (3) document or renumber the {1,2} labels. Note the -inf/-inf tie is the same degenerate-input class as quantwave-syjj.

title: Move talib-rs from [dependencies] to [dev-dependencies] — it is an oracle, not a runtime dep
description:
The indicators are native Rust now, but talib-rs is still declared under [dependencies] in quantwave-core/Cargo.toml, so every downstream `cargo add quantwave` pulls it into the build graph and the supply chain for a crate that is essentially a test oracle.

MEASURED USAGE (quantwave-core/src + quantwave-py/src, 176 refs total): exactly ONE runtime call in the library path, plus one bin. Everything else — 174 refs — is #[cfg(test)] parity assertions (the correct use of talib as an oracle) or the benchmark comparison.

KEEP THE BENCHMARKS. Benchmarking against talib-rs is deliberate and stays. Both #[cfg(test)] unit tests and benches/ can use dev-dependencies, so the oracle role survives the move intact. This issue is only about the dependency SECTION, not about deleting talib-rs.

THREE BLOCKERS, in increasing order of difficulty:

1. quantwave-core/src/indicators/incremental/bbands.rs:75 — the only runtime call. next_fallback() routes non-SMA matype to talib_rs::overlap::bbands over accumulated history. Worth fixing on its own merits regardless of this issue: it re-runs a batch computation across the full history on every bar, so it is O(n) per bar in a struct whose SMA path is O(1). Needs a native non-SMA path.

2. quantwave-core/src/bin/benchmark.rs — a normal bin target, and bin targets CANNOT use dev-dependencies. Note it is auto-discovered, not declared in [[bin]] (only benchmark_export and gen_gold_griffiths are). Move the talib comparison into benches/, where dev-deps are available and criterion already lives (quantwave-core/benches/indicator_throughput.rs). This preserves the benchmark, it just relocates it. Same check needed for the other auto-discovered bins in src/bin/ (bench_complex, bench_ema, bench_rust, bench_sma).

3. THE REAL BLOCKER — talib_rs::MaType leaks into the PUBLIC API. 121 references, including public struct fields and public constructors across apo, bbands, ma_stream, macd_ext, mavp, stoch and others, e.g. `pub matype: MaType` and `pub fn new(..., matype: MaType)`. A dev-dependency cannot appear in a public signature. This requires defining a native MaType enum in quantwave-core and converting at the test/bench boundary, and it is a BREAKING change for Rust API users. Python users are unaffected (they pass strings/ints).

Sequencing: (1) and (2) are independent and non-breaking, do them first. (3) is breaking and should ride a minor version bump with a changelog entry and a From/Into shim for the talib type at the test boundary.

Payoff: smaller dependency tree and faster cold builds for every downstream user, no third-party C-lineage crate in the shipped graph, and the "221 native indicators" claim becomes literally true of the dependency manifest and not just the implementations.
close_reason:
DONE. talib-rs is out of the shipped dependency graph, verified by cargo tree -e normal: 0 occurrences in quantwave-core, quantwave-polars, quantwave-py, quantwave and quantwave-backtest. It stays in dev-dependencies as the parity oracle for cfg(test) and the baseline for benches/talib_comparison - both deliberate and unchanged (cargo tree -e dev shows 1).

All three recorded blockers cleared: BBANDS runtime call (quantwave-3nyh); src/bin/benchmark.rs relocated to benches/talib_comparison.rs under criterion, since bin targets cannot use dev-dependencies, with all four measurements preserved and now statistically sampled; and talib_rs MaType removed from the public API in favour of a native enum (BREAKING for Rust callers, Python unaffected).

THIS ISSUE UNDERCOUNTED THE REAL BLOCKER. It claimed exactly one runtime call. There were 61: the bbands one plus 60 candlestick patterns calling talib_rs on EVERY BAR through the native_cdl macro in talib_wrapper.rs. A naive grep for talib_rs::x::y with parentheses missed them because the function is passed as a MACRO ARGUMENT - which is precisely how they stayed hidden. All 60 are now native O(1) streaming implementations; native_cdl and the 11 dead talib_ macros are deleted; the count is 0.

Seven implementations were found genuinely wrong while porting and fixed: CDL3WHITESOLDIERS, CDLADVANCEBLOCK, CDLHIKKAKE, CDLGAPSIDESIDEWHITE, CDLCONCEALBABYSWALL, CDL3STARSINSOUTH, CDLBREAKAWAY. Four were passing their tests only because their fixtures satisfied both the native and the oracle reading at once; fixtures were tightened and each fix mutation-verified.

Test integrity was the enabling work: the original proptest generator built bars independently, so rare multi-bar patterns never fired and their parity tests compared all-zeros to all-zeros - a deliberately broken implementation passed. The harness now uses a correlated random walk plus 36 hand-built positive fixtures and asserts the oracle actually produced signals.

Two patterns carry documented oracle exemptions because talib-rs itself is defective: CDL3BLACKCROWS (window seeded one bar early then rolled, becoming non-contiguous) and CDLHIKKAKEMOD (from bar 14 the oracle sums six terms and divides by five, with bar index 2 pinned permanently). Both keep exact next_batch-vs-streaming and bounded-memory checks plus an exact pin on the deterministic reference walk, so a regression cannot hide behind the exemption. CAVEAT: no ground-truth C TA-Lib was available, so native-equals-real-C-TA-Lib rests on a reconstructed model for those two.

Verified on main 3b667bfdd: 1107 tests, clippy -D warnings clean, rustfmt clean, 15/15 doc gate, 443 pytest, 221 indicators, CI green. The 221-native-indicators claim is now literally true and updated across README, llms.txt, comparison.md, faq.md, index.md, capability_matrix.md and pyproject.toml. Scope note: talib-rs was also dropped from quantwave-py/Cargo.toml, where it was declared with zero references and riding into the shipped wheel unused.

title: atr: list-API vs plugin disagree under one slug, and the EMA variant has no recorded source
description:
Split out of quantwave-l2n4, which covers documenting the convention. This one covers changing the behaviour, which l2n4 raises but leaves open.

Verified against 0.7.0 on identical inputs: atr(high, low, 14) = 2.916451, ta_atr(high, low, 14) = 3.496143 -- a ~20 percent gap. ta_atr matches TA-Lib exactly (Wilder RMA, SMA-seeded); atr matches neither TA-Lib, pandas-Wilder, nor SMA-ATR. Anyone reaching for the obvious name gets the unconventional variant, and ATR feeds stop distance and vol-target position sizing, so a 20 percent error propagates directly into risk.

The name atr carries a strong industry expectation of Wilder. Deliverables (decision needed): (a) make atr Wilder-by-default and preserve the current implementation under an explicit slug -- breaking, needs a gold-standard revalidation and a changelog entry; (b) keep both and make the divergence impossible to miss via metadata/boundary_info plus a docs callout; (c) deprecate the bare atr name in favour of two explicit slugs. Prefer (a) or (c) -- (b) leaves a footgun that only reading the docs defuses. Whichever lands, the same audit should sweep the catalog for other slugs whose name implies a convention they do not follow.
notes:
LEAD, partially verified 2026-08-02. A second agent flagged 'which surface labels Aroon Up/Down correctly' as a finding but died mid-verification. I checked it: BOTH surfaces are internally correct, so this is not a mislabelling bug.

  pl.col('high').ta.aroon('low',14) on a rising series -> {'down': 0.0, 'up': 100.0}   CORRECT (named struct)
  quantwave.talib.AROON(h,l,14)     on a rising series -> ([0]=0.0, [1]=100.0)          CORRECT per TA-Lib

The real trap is TUPLE ORDER on the talib surface: TA-Lib's AROON returns (aroondown, aroonup) -- down FIRST -- which is the opposite of what the name 'Aroon Up/Down' leads people to unpack. up, down = talib.AROON(...) silently swaps them. The plugin avoids this by returning a named struct, so the two surfaces disagree in ergonomics even though both are correct.

This belongs in the same catalog sweep as the rest of this issue: slugs whose name or return shape implies a convention they do not follow. Worth documenting on the talib-migration guide. Not yet checked: the list-based qw.ta.aroon returns an opaque AroonResult object whose field order/naming was not inspected, and the streaming class takes next(high, low) as two positional args rather than a tuple, unlike other multi-input streaming indicators -- both worth a look when this issue is picked up.
close_reason:
Shipped convention discoverability. quantwave-core/src/indicators/conventions.rs (CONVENTION_NOTES) mirrored in Python as qw.conventions(name) / qw.convention_slugs() / ConventionNote, also on metadata(name).conventions and boundary_info(name).conventions; empty for most indicators, 8 slugs carry notes (atr, atr_ts, keltner, roc, stddev, supertrend, ttm_squeeze, vpn — the last five inheriting the EMA-smoothed ATR). Per the AGENTS.md source rule, unestablished provenance is recorded as 'NONE RECORDED' rather than assuming a source; that is the case for the EMA ATR variant, whose recorded formula_source and LaTeX both describe Wilder's RMA (what ta_atr implements). No indicator math changed.

PREMISE CORRECTED: the Polars plugin .ta.atr IS Wilder and matches TA-Lib, as does quantwave.talib.ATR. Only the Atr streaming class and the native atr() batch function use the EMA variant. The original 3.496143 evidence came from calling ta_atr in the wrong argument order — see quantwave-sww3 (P0).

CATALOG SWEEP COMPLETE: all 10 ta_*/non-prefixed twins compared numerically on the plugin surface — atr, natr, trange, beta, correl, linearreg{,_angle,_intercept,_slope}, tsf. Every pair matches at equal periods, so the plugin surface carries no formula divergence. Sweep did surface a separate silent issue: twins disagree on DEFAULT periods (correl 30 vs ta_correl 14, beta 5 vs ta_beta 14) — split to quantwave-0h4o. Aroon lead also resolved and recorded in this issue's notes: not a mislabelling, both surfaces correct, the trap is TA-Lib's (aroondown, aroonup) tuple order.

(they are gold-vector-validated, so they have no test_<slug>_parity against talib-rs), so
talib.RSI also fails.

SCOPE: bridge the pure-Rust TA-Lib functions (esp. the 61 CDL candlesticks) into quantwave-python
so quantwave.talib is a real, complete TA-Lib-compatible surface. Then fix the harvest/map so
gold-validated natives (rsi/macd/sma/...) are included too. Pre-existing; identical on main/uniffi;
orthogonal to 5ipk.10. Blocks the talib DX tests in quantwave-mgst.

title: execution_delay defaults to same_bar, which fills on the signal bar's own close
description: Verified against 0.7.0. backtest_with_report / backtest / portfolio_backtest all default execution_delay="same_bar", which fills at the close of the very bar that produced the signal. When the signal is derived from that same close -- which is the overwhelmingly common case, e.g. (rsi < 30) computed on bar t -- the fill uses information available only at the instant the bar ends. Repro: identical signal frame, same_bar entered at 100.5, next_bar at 101.0 on a rising series; the default is systematically the more favourable side. This is not flagged, warned, or defaulted against, so every quickstart-shaped backtest silently reports optimistic entries. Deliverables (decision needed): (a) flip the default to next_bar and treat as a breaking change with a changelog entry, or (b) keep the default and emit a one-time warning when execution_delay is unset, or (c) require the caller to pass it explicitly. Option (a) is preferred -- the safe default should be the honest one. Whichever lands, document the semantics in the backtest quickstart alongside the signal convention.
close_reason:
execution_delay now defaults to next_bar across all .bt entry points, ExecutionDelay::default(), BtOptions::default() and the pyo3 signature; same_bar remains available explicitly. Breaking, changelog entry under [Unreleased]. Verified independently: 835 Rust tests pass, 390 Python pass, rustfmt_check.sh clean, and end-to-end default entry=101.0 (== next_bar) vs same_bar=100.5 on the same frame.

FOUND A SECOND, PRE-EXISTING BUG in the process: run_shared_capital_streaming_simulation never applied the execution delay at all — the batch path pre-shifts signals per timestamp group, the streaming path did not. Anyone explicitly passing next_bar silently got same-bar fills in streaming mode, breaking the headline batch<->streaming parity guarantee. Invisible while same_bar was the default. Fixed via apply_group_execution_delay, reusing the shared crate::signal_bar_index and defaulting absent symbols to flat to mirror the batch path's delayed_signals. Confirmed load-bearing: disabling it fails 5 parity tests including both shared-capital proptests; shrunk seeds checked in as portfolio_proptest_parity.proptest-regressions.

No test weakened. Most were pinned to SameBar explicitly to preserve their original intent (exact T+0 fill prices / cost arithmetic). Only two had expectations updated, both where the intent genuinely was 'the default': test_basic_long_only_flip_on_synthetic (close series re-picked so the trade wins under an honest T+1 fill rather than only under look-ahead) and test_t0_regression_default -> test_default_delay_is_next_bar. New test added pinning the pyo3 BacktestConfig default, which nothing covered since .bt always forwards the value explicitly. Commit 74f7d5448 on wip/quantwave-zmjw-execution-delay, not pushed.

title: Nightly benchmark frame_hash is not deterministic across numpy/polars versions
description:
Found while fixing quantwave-ss7q. Running benchmarks/harness.py on the same 1M-row config produces different frame_hash values on different environments: 838b3da4... on the system interpreter vs e7bff519... in a fresh venv with different numpy/polars minor versions.

frame_hash exists to prove the benchmark ran against identical data. If it moves with the dependency stack, it cannot serve that purpose, and benchmarks/results/latest.json will show spurious diffs every time the workflow's pip resolution shifts -- noise in a file that is committed back to main on every run.

Deliverable: make the generator version-independent (seed and draw through a pinned, explicit algorithm rather than whatever numpy default_rng or polars does this release), or drop frame_hash if it cannot be made meaningful.

title: quantwave-wasm pins getrandom 0.2 for a reason that no longer exists
description:
Found while investigating quantwave-mm67. quantwave-wasm/Cargo.toml:17-26 carries an explicit getrandom = { version = 0.2, features = [js] } workaround, commented as needed because quantwave-core pulls in rand v0.8 transitively via nalgebra.

That attribution is stale. nalgebra 0.35 is on rand 0.10 / getrandom 0.3, and cargo tree -p quantwave-wasm -i getrandom@0.2 returns nothing -- nothing pulls getrandom 0.2 any more except this pin itself. It is now dead weight forcing an old getrandom into the wasm build.

Deliverable: remove the pin, confirm the wasm target still builds and its tests pass, and delete the stale comment.
